claim: Intrinsically disordered regions make up a large part of the proteome.
source: Intrinsically disordered regions make up a large part of the proteome, but the sequence-to-function relationship in these regions is poorly understood, in part because the primary amino acid sequences of these regions are poorly conserved in alignments.
evidence: This is a general statement about IDRs in the abstract, supported by established scientific knowledge about proteome composition.

claim: The sequence-to-function relationship in intrinsically disordered regions is poorly understood.
source: Intrinsically disordered regions make up a large part of the proteome, but the sequence-to-function relationship in these regions is poorly understood, in part because the primary amino acid sequences of these regions are poorly conserved in alignments.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field as described in the abstract.

claim: The primary amino acid sequences of intrinsically disordered regions are poorly conserved in alignments.
source: Intrinsically disordered regions make up a large part of the proteome, but the sequence-to-function relationship in these regions is poorly understood, in part because the primary amino acid sequences of these regions are poorly conserved in alignments.
evidence: This is supported by citations throughout the manuscript and is a well-established observation in the field.

claim: Most disordered regions contain multiple molecular features that are preserved.
source: We find that most disordered regions contain multiple molecular features that are preserved, and we define these as 'evolutionary signatures' of disordered regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the proteome-wide evolutionary analysis presented in the results.

claim: Intrinsically disordered regions with similar evolutionary signatures can rescue function in vivo.
source: We demonstrate that intrinsically disordered regions with similar evolutionary signatures can rescue function in vivo, and that groups of intrinsically disordered regions with similar evolutionary signatures are strongly enriched for functional annotations and phenotypes.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data with Ste50 IDR replacements and mitochondrial targeting signal experiments.

claim: Groups of intrinsically disordered regions with similar evolutionary signatures are strongly enriched for functional annotations and phenotypes.
source: We demonstrate that intrinsically disordered regions with similar evolutionary signatures can rescue function in vivo, and that groups of intrinsically disordered regions with similar evolutionary signatures are strongly enriched for functional annotations and phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis and enrichment tests presented in the results section.

claim: Evolutionary signatures can be used to predict function for many disordered regions from their amino acid sequences.
source: We propose that evolutionary signatures can be used to predict function for many disordered regions from their amino acid sequences.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the findings of the study, representing an inference from the data presented.

claim: Intrinsically disordered protein regions are associated with cell signaling.
source: Intrinsically disordered protein regions are associated with a large array of functions (reviewed in Forman-Kay and Mittag, 2013), including cell signaling (Iakoucheva et al., 2004; Tompa, 2014; Wright and Dyson, 2015), mediation of protein-protein interactions (Borgia et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2012; Tompa et al., 2015), and the formation of membraneless organelles through phase separation (Banani et al., 2017; Franzmann et al., 2018; Nott et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015; Riback et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Intrinsically disordered protein regions are associated with mediation of protein-protein interactions.
source: Intrinsically disordered protein regions are associated with a large array of functions (reviewed in Forman-Kay and Mittag, 2013), including cell signaling (Iakoucheva et al., 2004; Tompa, 2014; Wright and Dyson, 2015), mediation of protein-protein interactions (Borgia et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2012; Tompa et al., 2015), and the formation of membraneless organelles through phase separation (Banani et al., 2017; Franzmann et al., 2018; Nott et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015; Riback et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Intrinsically disordered protein regions are associated with the formation of membraneless organelles through phase separation.
source: Intrinsically disordered protein regions are associated with a large array of functions (reviewed in Forman-Kay and Mittag, 2013), including cell signaling (Iakoucheva et al., 2004; Tompa, 2014; Wright and Dyson, 2015), mediation of protein-protein interactions (Borgia et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2012; Tompa et al., 2015), and the formation of membraneless organelles through phase separation (Banani et al., 2017; Franzmann et al., 2018; Nott et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015; Riback et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Intrinsically disordered regions are widespread in eukaryotic proteomes.
source: These regions are widespread in eukaryotic proteomes (Peng et al., 2013; Ward et al., 2004), but do not fold into stable secondary or tertiary structures, and do not typically perform enzymatic functions (Uversky, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Intrinsically disordered regions do not fold into stable secondary or tertiary structures.
source: These regions are widespread in eukaryotic proteomes (Peng et al., 2013; Ward et al., 2004), but do not fold into stable secondary or tertiary structures, and do not typically perform enzymatic functions (Uversky, 2011).
evidence: This is a defining characteristic of IDRs supported by citation.

claim: Intrinsically disordered regions do not typically perform enzymatic functions.
source: These regions are widespread in eukaryotic proteomes (Peng et al., 2013; Ward et al., 2004), but do not fold into stable secondary or tertiary structures, and do not typically perform enzymatic functions (Uversky, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Uversky, 2011.

claim: Intrinsically disordered regions can readily be identified based on their primary amino acid sequence.
source: Although intrinsically disordered regions can readily be identified based on their primary amino acid sequence (Dosztányi et al., 2005; Uversky, 2002), it remains a challenge to associate these regions with specific biological and biochemical functions based on their amino acid sequences, limiting systematic functional analysis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prediction methods.

claim: It remains a challenge to associate intrinsically disordered regions with specific biological and biochemical functions based on their amino acid sequences.
source: Although intrinsically disordered regions can readily be identified based on their primary amino acid sequence (Dosztányi et al., 2005; Uversky, 2002), it remains a challenge to associate these regions with specific biological and biochemical functions based on their amino acid sequences, limiting systematic functional analysis.
evidence: This represents the current state of the field and the motivation for the study.

claim: For folded regions, protein function can often be predicted with high specificity based on the presence of conserved protein domains.
source: In stark contrast, for folded regions, protein function can often be predicted with high specificity based on the presence of conserved protein domains (El-Gebali et al., 2019) or enzymatic active sites (Ondrechen et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to domain databases and active site prediction methods.

claim: Short segments of evolutionary conservation in otherwise rapidly evolving disordered regions point to key functional residues.
source: We and others (Davey et al., 2012; Nguyen Ba et al., 2012) have shown that short segments of evolutionary conservation in otherwise rapidly evolving disordered regions point to key functional residues, often important for posttranslational modifications, or other transient protein interactions (Tompa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors and others.

claim: Conserved segments in disordered regions are often important for posttranslational modifications or other transient protein interactions.
source: We and others (Davey et al., 2012; Nguyen Ba et al., 2012) have shown that short segments of evolutionary conservation in otherwise rapidly evolving disordered regions point to key functional residues, often important for posttranslational modifications, or other transient protein interactions (Tompa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tompa et al., 2014.

claim: Conserved segments make up a small fraction (5%) of disordered regions.
source: However, these conserved segments make up a small fraction of disordered regions (5%), and the vast majority of disordered amino acids show little evidence for evolutionary constraint in alignments of primary amino acid sequences (Colak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Colak et al., 2013.

claim: The vast majority of disordered amino acids show little evidence for evolutionary constraint in alignments of primary amino acid sequences.
source: However, these conserved segments make up a small fraction of disordered regions (5%), and the vast majority of disordered amino acids show little evidence for evolutionary constraint in alignments of primary amino acid sequences (Colak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Colak et al., 2013.

claim: More than 5000 intrinsically disordered regions were identified in the S. cerevisiae proteome.
source: We identified more than 5000 intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) in the S. cerevisiae proteome and quantified their evolutionary divergence (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct result from the computational analysis described in the methods.

claim: IDRs evolve more rapidly than regions that were not identified as disordered.
source: As expected, we found that the IDRs evolve more rapidly than the regions that were not identified as disordered (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The vast majority of IDRs are distinct from Pfam domains.
source: We also confirmed that the vast majority of these IDRs are distinct from Pfam domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 91% of IDRs have 0% Pfam overlap.
source: Percentage of regions with 0% Pfam overlap for IDRs is 91%, whereas for non-IDRs it is 74%.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Charge properties such as net charge and acidic residue content are most likely to deviate from the null expectation in more than 50% of IDRs.
source: We find that charge properties such as net charge and acidic residue content are most likely to deviate from our null expectation (more than 50% of IDRs) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Non-conserved motif density deviates from the null expectation in 21.6% of IDRs at most for CDK phosphorylation consensus sites.
source: This is in contrast to non-conserved motif density, which deviates from our null expectation in 21.6% of IDRs at most (for CDK phosphorylation consensus sites).
evidence: This is a result from the proteome-wide analysis.

claim: Sequence complexity deviates from the null expectation in 43.0% of IDRs.
source: Other molecular features that frequently deviate from our null expectation are sequence complexity (43.0%), asparagine residue content (43.3%), and physicochemical features such as isoelectric point (53.9%).
evidence: This is a result from the proteome-wide analysis.

claim: Asparagine residue content deviates from the null expectation in 43.3% of IDRs.
source: Other molecular features that frequently deviate from our null expectation are sequence complexity (43.0%), asparagine residue content (43.3%), and physicochemical features such as isoelectric point (53.9%).
evidence: This is a result from the proteome-wide analysis.

claim: Isoelectric point deviates from the null expectation in 53.9% of IDRs.
source: Other molecular features that frequently deviate from our null expectation are sequence complexity (43.0%), asparagine residue content (43.3%), and physicochemical features such as isoelectric point (53.9%).
evidence: This is a result from the proteome-wide analysis.

claim: The mean of each molecular feature deviates from the null expectation more often than the variance.
source: We also found that the mean of each molecular feature deviates from our null expectation more often than the variance (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Many IDRs have many significant molecular features, with a median of 15 significant molecular features per IDR.
source: Surprisingly, many IDRs have many significant molecular features, with a median of 15 significant molecular features per IDR (compared to one significant feature expected by chance; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a result from the proteome-wide analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: One significant feature is expected by chance per IDR.
source: Surprisingly, many IDRs have many significant molecular features, with a median of 15 significant molecular features per IDR (compared to one significant feature expected by chance; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is derived from the random expectation analysis described in the methods.

claim: The Ste50 IDR has five consensus phosphorylation sites that are implicated in its function.
source: While the Ste50 IDR has five consensus phosphorylation sites that are implicated in its function (Hao et al., 2008; Yamamoto et al., 2010; Zarin et al., 2017), the Pex5 IDR and Rad26 IDR have none, and the Stp4 IDR has 4.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Pex5 IDR has no consensus phosphorylation sites.
source: While the Ste50 IDR has five consensus phosphorylation sites that are implicated in its function (Hao et al., 2008; Yamamoto et al., 2010; Zarin et al., 2017), the Pex5 IDR and Rad26 IDR have none, and the Stp4 IDR has 4.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 2A.

claim: The Rad26 IDR has no consensus phosphorylation sites.
source: While the Ste50 IDR has five consensus phosphorylation sites that are implicated in its function (Hao et al., 2008; Yamamoto et al., 2010; Zarin et al., 2017), the Pex5 IDR and Rad26 IDR have none, and the Stp4 IDR has 4.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 2A.

claim: The Stp4 IDR has 4 consensus phosphorylation sites.
source: While the Ste50 IDR has five consensus phosphorylation sites that are implicated in its function (Hao et al., 2008; Yamamoto et al., 2010; Zarin et al., 2017), the Pex5 IDR and Rad26 IDR have none, and the Stp4 IDR has 4.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 2A.

claim: The basal mating reporter expression in each strain corresponded to how similar the evolutionary signature of the replacing IDR was to that of the Ste50 IDR.
source: We found that the basal mating reporter expression in each strain corresponded to how similar the evolutionary signature of the replacing IDR was to that of the Ste50 IDR (all mutants significantly different from wildtype and each other, Wilcoxon test p<0.05, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All mutants were significantly different from wildtype and each other (Wilcoxon test p<0.05).
source: We found that the basal mating reporter expression in each strain corresponded to how similar the evolutionary signature of the replacing IDR was to that of the Ste50 IDR (all mutants significantly different from wildtype and each other, Wilcoxon test p<0.05, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: The two chimaeric strains that were more similar in their evolutionary signatures to the wildtype (Pex5 and Stp4) began the process of shmooing.
source: We found that the two chimaeric strains that were more similar in their evolutionary signatures to the wildtype (Pex5 and Stp4) began the process of 'shmooing', or responding to pheromone, whereas the strain that had the IDR with the most different evolutionary signature (Rad 26) could not shmoo (Figure 2C; full micrographs in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The strain that had the IDR with the most different evolutionary signature (Rad26) could not shmoo.
source: We found that the two chimaeric strains that were more similar in their evolutionary signatures to the wildtype (Pex5 and Stp4) began the process of 'shmooing', or responding to pheromone, whereas the strain that had the IDR with the most different evolutionary signature (Rad 26) could not shmoo (Figure 2C; full micrographs in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The IDRs fall into at least 23 clusters based on similarity of their evolutionary signatures.
source: The IDRs fall into at least 23 clusters based on similarity of their evolutionary signatures (groups A through W, Figure 3) that are significantly associated with specific biological functions (enriched for Gene Ontology (GO) term, phenotype, and/or literature annotations, False Discovery Rate [FDR]=5%, Benjamini-Hochberg corrected) (Table 1; full table of enrichments in supplementary data; clustered IDRs and evolutionary signatures in supplementary data).
evidence: This is a result from the clustering analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The 23 clusters are significantly associated with specific biological functions (FDR=5%, Benjamini-Hochberg corrected).
source: The IDRs fall into at least 23 clusters based on similarity of their evolutionary signatures (groups A through W, Figure 3) that are significantly associated with specific biological functions (enriched for Gene Ontology (GO) term, phenotype, and/or literature annotations, False Discovery Rate [FDR]=5%, Benjamini-Hochberg corrected) (Table 1; full table of enrichments in supplementary data; clustered IDRs and evolutionary signatures in supplementary data).
evidence: This is a result from the enrichment analysis.

claim: Cluster M is associated with nucleocytoplasmic transporter activity and includes IDRs from FG-NUP proteins.
source: For example, we find a cluster that is associated with 'nucleocytoplasmic transporter activity' (cluster M) that includes IDRs from FG-NUP proteins Nup42, Nup145, Nup57, Nup49, Nup116, and Nup100 that form part of the nuclear pore central transport channel (Alber et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the clustering and enrichment analysis, with citation to previous work.

claim: Cluster M contains molecular features such as increased asparagine content, increased polar residue content, and increased proline and charged residue demixing ('Omega').
source: In cluster M, we find molecular features such as increased asparagine content, increased polar residue content, and increased proline and charged residue demixing ('Omega'; Martin et al., 2016) in addition to the well-known 'FG' repeats that are found in the FG-NUP IDRs (reviewed in Terry and Wente, 2009).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of evolutionary signatures in cluster M.

claim: Cluster O contains IDRs from proteins associated with phase separation and membraneless organelles such as Sup35 and Dhh1.
source: Cluster O contains IDRs from proteins associated with phase separation and membraneless organelles such as Sup35 (Franzmann et al., 2018) and Dhh1 (Protter et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on these proteins.

claim: The evolutionary signatures for the IDRs in cluster O include features that are typically associated with 'prionogenic', low complexity disordered regions, such as increased mean polyglutamine repeats.
source: The evolutionary signatures for the IDRs in this cluster include features that are typically associated with so-called 'prionogenic', low complexity disordered regions, such as increased mean polyglutamine repeats (Alberti et al., 2009), but also indicate that there are other relevant molecular features for this set of disordered regions (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4A and citation to Alberti et al., 2009.

claim: In cluster O IDRs, the variance of the net charge is reduced, and charged residues are depleted during evolution.
source: For example, in these regions, the variance of the net charge is reduced, and charged residues are depleted during evolution.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of evolutionary signatures in cluster O.

claim: Cluster D is associated with DNA repair.
source: For example, cluster D (Figure 5A) is associated with DNA repair, and its evolutionary signature contains increased mean 'Kappa' (Das and Pappu, 2013) and decreased mean 'Sequence Charge Decoration' (SCD) (Sawle and Ghosh, 2015), both of which indicate that there is an increased separation of positive and negatively charged residues in these IDRs compared to our null expectation.
evidence: This is supported by the enrichment analysis for cluster D.

claim: Cluster D's evolutionary signature contains increased mean 'Kappa' and decreased mean 'Sequence Charge Decoration' (SCD), indicating increased separation of positive and negatively charged residues.
source: For example, cluster D (Figure 5A) is associated with DNA repair, and its evolutionary signature contains increased mean 'Kappa' (Das and Pappu, 2013) and decreased mean 'Sequence Charge Decoration' (SCD) (Sawle and Ghosh, 2015), both of which indicate that there is an increased separation of positive and negatively charged residues in these IDRs compared to our null expectation.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of evolutionary signatures in cluster D, with citations to the definitions of these features.

claim: The evolutionary signature for cluster D reveals an increased mean fraction of charged residues and negatively charged residues in particular.
source: The evolutionary signature for this cluster also reveals an increased mean fraction of charged residues and negatively charged residues in particular (Figure 5A), which is also clear in the comparison between the real Srs2 orthologs and the simulation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Three clusters (A, C, F) are associated with ribosome biogenesis.
source: For example, we find three clusters associated with ribosome biogenesis (clusters A, C, F) that cannot be distinguished based on their enriched GO terms.
evidence: This is a result from the enrichment analysis.

claim: In cluster A, 201/295 proteins have a 'nucleus' annotation.
source: The largest of these is cluster A, where 201/295 proteins have a 'nucleus' annotation, and 110/295 are essential proteins ('inviable' deletion phenotype).
evidence: This is a result from the enrichment analysis for cluster A.

claim: In cluster A, 110/295 are essential proteins ('inviable' deletion phenotype).
source: The largest of these is cluster A, where 201/295 proteins have a 'nucleus' annotation, and 110/295 are essential proteins ('inviable' deletion phenotype).
evidence: This is a result from the enrichment analysis for cluster A.

claim: Cluster A contains highly acidic IDRs with CKII phosphorylation consensus sites.
source: Cluster A contains highly acidic IDRs with CKII phosphorylation consensus sites.
evidence: This is a description of the molecular features in cluster A.

claim: CKII has been previously associated with nucleolar organization.
source: CKII has been previously associated with nucleolar organization (Louvet et al., 2006), and a previous analysis of non-conserved consensus phosphorylation sites found ribosome biogenesis as strongly enriched in predicted CKII targets (Lai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A previous analysis found ribosome biogenesis as strongly enriched in predicted CKII targets.
source: CKII has been previously associated with nucleolar organization (Louvet et al., 2006), and a previous analysis of non-conserved consensus phosphorylation sites found ribosome biogenesis as strongly enriched in predicted CKII targets (Lai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lai et al., 2012.

claim: Cluster C contains increased mean polylysine repeats.
source: Interestingly, cluster C contains increased mean polylysine repeats, and is significantly enriched for proteins that have been experimentally verified as targets for lysine polyphosphorylation (Bentley-DeSousa et al., 2018) (p=2.7×10−3, hypergeometric test).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of evolutionary signatures in cluster C.

claim: Cluster C is significantly enriched for proteins that have been experimentally verified as targets for lysine polyphosphorylation (p=2.7×10−3, hypergeometric test).
source: Interestingly, cluster C contains increased mean polylysine repeats, and is significantly enriched for proteins that have been experimentally verified as targets for lysine polyphosphorylation (Bentley-DeSousa et al., 2018) (p=2.7×10−3, hypergeometric test).
evidence: This is a result from enrichment analysis with citation to experimental data.

claim: Multiple clusters (I, J, L, N, O, R) have distinct evolutionary signatures enriched for terms associated with regulation of transcription.
source: We find similar observations in multiple clusters that have distinct evolutionary signatures enriched for terms associated with regulation of transcription (clusters I, J, L, N, O, R).
evidence: This is a result from the enrichment analysis.

claim: Clusters J, O and N have increased glutamine residue content.
source: For example, clusters J, O and N have increased glutamine residue content, and cluster N has increased proline residue content.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of evolutionary signatures.

claim: Cluster N has increased proline residue content.
source: For example, clusters J, O and N have increased glutamine residue content, and cluster N has increased proline residue content.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of evolutionary signatures.

claim: Clusters I and R have no amino acid composition bias.
source: However, clusters I and R have no amino acid composition bias, while cluster N has increased proline-directed phosphorylation consensus sites, suggesting post-translational modifications.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of evolutionary signatures.

claim: Cluster N has increased proline-directed phosphorylation consensus sites.
source: However, clusters I and R have no amino acid composition bias, while cluster N has increased proline-directed phosphorylation consensus sites, suggesting post-translational modifications.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of evolutionary signatures.

claim: Cluster W is exceptionally strongly associated with the mitochondrion (144/165 proteins in the cluster).
source: One of our clusters of intrinsically disordered regions is exceptionally strongly associated with the mitochondrion (144/165 proteins in the cluster) and other annotations that are related to mitochondrial localization and function (for example, 81/165 proteins in the cluster have shown a decreased respiratory growth phenotype) (Table 1, cluster W; see supplementary data for full list of significant enrichments).
evidence: This is a result from the enrichment analysis for cluster W.

claim: 81/165 proteins in cluster W have shown a decreased respiratory growth phenotype.
source: One of our clusters of intrinsically disordered regions is exceptionally strongly associated with the mitochondrion (144/165 proteins in the cluster) and other annotations that are related to mitochondrial localization and function (for example, 81/165 proteins in the cluster have shown a decreased respiratory growth phenotype) (Table 1, cluster W; see supplementary data for full list of significant enrichments).
evidence: This is a result from the enrichment analysis for cluster W.

claim: 145/165 of the disordered regions in cluster W are N-terminal.
source: Since 145/165 of the disordered regions in this cluster are N-terminal, we hypothesized that this cluster contains disordered regions that are associated with mitochondrial targeting signals (Vögtle et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of cluster W.

claim: Mitochondrial N-terminal targeting signals are depleted of negatively charged residues, have an abundance of positively charged residues, and are much more hydrophobic than the null expectation.
source: In line with this hypothesis, we find previously described sequence features of mitochondrial N-terminal targeting signals in our evolutionary signatures; for example, these IDRs are depleted of negatively charged residues, have an abundance of positively charged residues, and are much more hydrophobic than our null expectation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) (Garg and Gould, 2016; Vögtle et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and citations to previous studies.

claim: The IDRs in cluster W have a much higher probability of being mitochondrial targeting signals than any other cluster with enriched annotations (Bonferroni-corrected p≤6.5×10−11, Wilcoxon test).
source: Using this tool, we find that the IDRs in cluster W have a much higher probability of being mitochondrial targeting signals than any other cluster with enriched annotations in our analysis (Bonferroni-corrected p≤6.5×10−11, Wilcoxon test) (Figure 6B, red box).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: GFP-tagged Cox15 correctly localizes to the mitochondria when its disordered region is swapped with that of Atm1.
source: In accordance with our hypothesis, we find that GFP-tagged Cox15 correctly localizes to the mitochondria when its disordered region is swapped with that of Atm1, but does not localize correctly when its disordered region is deleted (Figure 6C; full micrographs in Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: GFP-tagged Cox15 does not localize correctly when its disordered region is deleted.
source: In accordance with our hypothesis, we find that GFP-tagged Cox15 correctly localizes to the mitochondria when its disordered region is swapped with that of Atm1, but does not localize correctly when its disordered region is deleted (Figure 6C; full micrographs in Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: When the Cox15 IDR is replaced with the Emp47 IDR, there is no mitochondrial localization of Cox15-GFP.
source: Next, we replaced the Cox15 IDR with the disordered region of Emp47, which has an evolutionary signature that we predict to be associated with targeting signals for the endoplasmic reticulum (cluster V). In this case, as we predicted, we found no mitochondrial localization of Cox15-GFP.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data.

claim: Restoring the wildtype N-terminal IDR rescues mitochondrial localization in strains where the Cox15 IDR was replaced with Emp47 or knocked out.
source: Therefore, we restored the wildtype N-terminal IDR in the strains in which the Cox15 IDR was replaced with Emp47 or knocked out (Figure 6—figure supplement 4). Because we were able to rescue the mitochondrial localization with the restored wildtype IDR, we conclude that the absence of mitochondrial GFP expression is directly linked to the mutations we made in the N-terminal IDR of each strain.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Rnq1 falls into the cluster of disordered regions associated with nucleocytoplasmic transport (cluster M).
source: Interestingly, Rnq1 falls into our cluster of disordered regions that are associated with nucleocytoplasmic transport (cluster M) and the nuclear pore central transport channel.
evidence: This is a result from the clustering analysis.

claim: An RNQ1 deletion was shown to cause nuclear aggregation of the polyQ-expanded huntingtin exon1 (Httex1) in a model of Huntington's disease.
source: While Rnq1 is annotated with a cytosolic localization, an RNQ1 deletion was recently shown to cause nuclear aggregation of the polyQ-expanded huntingtin exon1 (Httex1) in a model of Huntington's disease (Zheng et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2017.

claim: Predictions of function based on cluster annotations clearly matched the gene description of the proteins in 5 of 10 cases for the most disordered yeast proteins with known functions.
source: We found that predictions of function based on our cluster annotations clearly matched the gene description of the proteins in 5 of 10 cases, suggesting a predictive power of at least 50% (Supplementary file 1 - Table S3, see Discussion).
evidence: This is a result from the validation analysis.

claim: The lack of constraint on primary amino acid sequence alignments in disordered regions is relative compared to folded regions.
source: In contrast to the relative lack of constraint on primary amino acid sequence alignments (compared to folded regions, Brown et al., 2002; Tóth-Petróczy and Tawfik, 2013), we find that the vast majority of disordered regions contain molecular features that deviate in their evolution from our null expectation (a simulation of disordered region evolution; Nguyen Ba et al., 2014; Nguyen Ba et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and the current study's findings.

claim: The vast majority of disordered regions contain molecular features that deviate in their evolution from the null expectation.
source: In contrast to the relative lack of constraint on primary amino acid sequence alignments (compared to folded regions, Brown et al., 2002; Tóth-Petróczy and Tawfik, 2013), we find that the vast majority of disordered regions contain molecular features that deviate in their evolution from our null expectation (a simulation of disordered region evolution; Nguyen Ba et al., 2014; Nguyen Ba et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: The evidence for constraint on IDRs represents a lower bound on the total amount of functional constraint on highly diverged IDRs.
source: Thus, our evidence for constraint must represent a lower bound on the total amount of functional constraint on highly diverged IDRs: there are very likely to be sequence characteristics that were not captured by our features.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of the feature set used.

claim: The lack of homology between most IDRs with similar evolutionary signatures suggests that the molecular features are preserved in each IDR independently.
source: The lack of homology between most IDRs with similar evolutionary signatures suggests that the molecular features are preserved in each IDR independently.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of similar evolutionary signatures without sequence similarity.

claim: The more than 150 IDRs that represent mitochondrial N-terminal targeting signals share similar constraints on their molecular features, yet these signals have been preserved independently over very long evolutionary time.
source: For example, the more than 150 IDRs that we believe represent mitochondrial N-terminal targeting signals share similar constraints on their molecular features, yet these signals have been preserved independently over very long evolutionary time as mitochondrial genes were transferred individually to the nuclear genome (Adams and Palmer, 2003).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Adams and Palmer, 2003.

claim: The preservation of molecular features over long evolutionary time, despite accumulation of amino acid divergence, is consistent with a model of stabilizing selection.
source: The preservation of molecular features over long evolutionary time, despite accumulation of amino acid divergence, is consistent with a model of stabilizing selection (Bedford and Hartl, 2009; Hansen, 1997; Lande, 1976), where individual amino acid sites are under relatively weak functional constraints (Landry et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to evolutionary theory.

claim: Single point mutations in IDRs are unlikely to dramatically impair IDR function.
source: In this view, single point mutations are unlikely to dramatically impair IDR function, and therefore large evolutionary divergence can accumulate.
evidence: This is an inference from the stabilizing selection model.

claim: Disease-causing mutations in disordered regions are more likely to cause gain of function.
